titre: Dimetrodon Is Not a Dinosaur: It Is Closer to Us
accroche: The sailed reptile of children's books died out well before the first dinosaurs. It belongs to the mammal lineage.
contenu_vulgarise:
In children's books and toy boxes, Dimetrodon almost always appears among the dinosaurs: a large four-legged animal, a mouth full of teeth, a sail on its back. Yet this is the most widespread misconception in popular paleontology. Dimetrodon is not a dinosaur, and it is not even, strictly speaking, a reptile.

## Another Branch of the Tree

Amniotes, the vertebrates that lay an egg with a shell or membranes, split very early into two great lineages. On one side, the sauropsids, which include lizards, crocodiles, dinosaurs and birds. On the other, the synapsids, of which today's mammals are the only survivors. Dimetrodon belongs to the synapsids: it is closer to a mammal than to any reptile, living or extinct. That is the point of the title of a 2009 article by Kenneth Angielczyk: “Dimetrodon is not a dinosaur.”

## A World Without Dinosaurs

Dimetrodon lived in the Permian, roughly 294 to 271 million years ago according to Wikipedia. Smithsonian Magazine places its peak at around 280 to 265 million years ago and specifies that it predates the first dinosaurs by at least 35 million years; Angielczyk's article puts that gap at about 60 million years. When Tyrannosaurus rex walks North America, Dimetrodon has been gone for more than two hundred million years. The word “reptile” is confusing here: according to Smithsonian Magazine, the synapsid lineage split from the sauropsid lineage more than 324 million years ago, long before dinosaurs appeared.

## Why the Name Misled

Edward Drinker Cope named Dimetrodon in 1878. The name means “two measures of tooth,” an allusion to its teeth of two sizes, which is a mammalian trait rather than a reptilian one. The expression “mammal-like reptile” long referred to these animals, but Angielczyk's article judges it misleading and outdated: synapsids and reptiles are two distinct lineages descended from a common ancestor, and neither descends from the other. Dimetrodon's sail, carried on long spines from its vertebrae, also fed the confusion. The hypothesis of temperature regulation is now debated, and a display function is judged more likely. A 2010 study goes further and proposes that sexual selection was the main driver of the evolution of this sail, rather than a thermal need.

repere.texte: Dimetrodon lived in the Permian, roughly 294 to 271 million years ago. It died out at least 35 million years before the first dinosaurs, up to 60 million years according to another estimate. It belongs to the synapsids, the mammal lineage, and not to the sauropsids, the lineage of reptiles, dinosaurs and birds.
repere.source: Angielczyk, Evolution: Education and Outreach, 2009; Smithsonian Magazine

carte.punch: Dimetrodon is not a dinosaur: it is closer to you than to a crocodile.
carte.idee: The sailed reptile of children's books is a synapsid: it belongs to the mammal lineage. It died out tens of millions of years before the first dinosaurs appeared.

quiz.question: Why is Dimetrodon not a dinosaur?
choix: It lived in the sea, whereas dinosaurs were land animals
It belongs to the mammal lineage and died out well before the dinosaurs
It is too small to be placed in this animal group
It is a giant lizard that appeared long after the dinosaurs
quiz.explication: Dimetrodon is a synapsid, from the lineage that leads to mammals, and it lived in the Permian, tens of millions of years before the first dinosaurs. It lived on land, it could be very large, and it did not come after the dinosaurs.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does the name “Dimetrodon,” given by Edward Drinker Cope in 1878, mean?
choix: Sail lizard, referring to the animal's dorsal crest
Big eater, referring to its size and appetite
Two measures of tooth, referring to its teeth of two sizes
First reptile, referring to its discovery in the Permian
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The name means two measures of tooth, an allusion to its teeth of two different sizes, a trait that the text links to mammals rather than reptiles.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does a 2010 study propose about Dimetrodon's dorsal sail?
choix: That it mainly served to swim faster in the wetlands of the Permian, according to this study
That sexual selection was its main driver, rather than a need for thermoregulation
That it gradually disappeared well before the species went fully extinct, according to this study
That it allowed the animal to glide over short distances, according to this 2010 study
quiz_supplementaire.explication: A 2010 study proposes that sexual selection was the main driver of the sail's evolution, rather than thermal regulation, a hypothesis now debated.
